item.title: Five Days to 50%: Inside the New Tariff Deadline Squeezing Canada, Brazil and 60 Other Trading Partners
item.body:
Two trade actions that have been building quietly for weeks are now converging on a single, consequential date. Starting August 19, a 50% tariff on a wide swath of Canadian goods takes effect, layering on top of tariffs already imposed on Brazil and dozens of other countries over forced-labor concerns in global supply chains. Together, the two measures touch products from dairy and wine to furniture, motor vehicles and clothing — and they rely on legal authority the United States has almost never used in this way before.

## The Canada Deadline: August 19

In late July, the White House signed proclamations invoking Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a Depression-era provision that lets the president impose additional duties of up to 50% on goods from a country found to discriminate against U.S. commerce. It is a tool with almost no modern precedent — and it is now set to apply a 50% surcharge to a specific list of Canadian imports beginning August 19.

The headline categories are dairy, alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles, but trade advisories describe a longer list that also includes wine, furniture, plywood, cement, hockey sticks, fishing rods, seeds and clothing. Notably, goods that normally qualify for duty-free treatment under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) are not exempt from this new tariff — origin under the trade pact does not shield covered products from the Section 338 duty.

Trade groups estimate the exposure at roughly $20 billion, a slice of the more than $380 billion in goods the U.S. imported from Canada last year. For companies that source dairy ingredients, packaged alcohol or finished furniture from Canadian suppliers, the deadline leaves only days to adjust purchasing plans, renegotiate contracts, or absorb the added cost.

## The Forced-Labor Tariffs: 60 Countries, Two Rates

Running alongside the Canada action is a separate and broader measure. Earlier this summer, the U.S. Trade Representative's office released findings from Section 301 investigations into 60 trading economies, examining whether each country bans — and effectively enforces bans on — imports made with forced labor. The conclusion: most fell short, and USTR proposed new tariffs as a result.

Under the rollout, roughly a dozen economies that maintain at least a partial prohibition or have committed to reciprocal-trade enforcement steps face a 10% tariff, while the majority of the 60 countries face a steeper 12.5% rate. Brazil is among the economies assigned the higher tier; its government has publicly pushed back, calling the action unjustified. Unlike the Canada tariffs, which take effect August 19, the forced-labor duties began landing on shipments in late July, meaning many importers are already absorbing the cost.

## Why Now, and Why These Tools

Both actions share a common thread: each relies on a legal mechanism that has sat largely dormant for decades. Section 338 has essentially never been used to impose duties at this scale, while Section 301's forced-labor framing marks a shift from its more familiar role in disputes over intellectual property or subsidies. Trade attorneys tracking the rollout note that the unusual legal basis for both measures could make them targets for legal challenges or future negotiation, even as they take effect on schedule for now.

## What It Means Going Forward

For everyday consumers, the near-term effect is likely to show up gradually — in the price of Canadian cheese, whisky and furniture, and in goods imported from the 60 affected economies, from apparel to electronics components. For businesses, the bigger challenge is the compressed timeline: importers have had only weeks, not months, to map which SKUs are covered, recalculate landed costs and decide whether to pass increases on to customers.

Because tariff schedules, product exclusion lists and country-specific rates can change on short notice — through litigation, bilateral talks or further executive action — businesses and consumers with a direct stake in these categories should verify current requirements through official U.S. Trade Representative and Customs and Border Protection guidance, or with qualified trade counsel, rather than relying on any single news summary. The situation remains fluid, and the coming days are likely to bring further clarification from both Washington and the affected trading partners.
